outliers.text:
Spotify cut their Claude Code token bill by 90%.

Then they open-sourced how they did it.

The insight underneath is almost boring: coding agents spend most of the bill on reading:

A coding agent will read a 4,000 line file just to answer a question about a single function.

All this reading done by a frontier model that's wildly overqualified for it.

Here's the breakdown. Save it before your next agent run:

1️⃣ Expensive models shouldn't read.
↳ Use a hook to block full reads of any file over 350 lines.
↳ Have a cheap worker read it instead and hand back only the answer.

2️⃣ The savings are biggest on large files.
↳ On a 162K line Java monorepo, they saw 82 to 94% fewer tokens.

Succinctness makes a product strategy shine.

I think there is too much concern expressed about the need for human verification of AI output in everyday work due to a risk of factual errors. It used to be true, but data on more recent models suggest they beat human experts in finding facts & checking claims. AIs may still underperform humans in error rates in some cases, of course, but we need to update our assumptions about how often that occurs.

And there are things to verify beyond errors - points of view, opinions, approaches, etc. But the idea that the job of humans should be checking AI work for mistakes is likely already not true today, and good riddance.

Today we’re introducing ParseBench-2 - our most ambitious document parsing benchmark to date.

It is the only benchmark that provides both extreme granularity into every single type of production parsing error, while also making sure that metric scores are highly aligned with human judgment. We do this by painstakingly assigning severity scores to 330+ error types, and tuning each metric to match the severity scores. 
Existing benchmarks either use brittle deterministic metrics (e.g. OmniDocBench) or LLM-as-a-judge (ParseArena), which can help recognize equivalent representations but are coarse/stochastic/subject to bias by the prompt+model.

ParseBench-2 also contains:
✅ 4.3k+ document page

LinkedIn has published one of the best reports I’ve read on deploying LLM applications: what worked and what didn’t.

1. Structured outputs
They chose YAML over JSON as the output format because YAML uses less output tokens. Initially, only 90% of the outputs are correctly formatted YAML. They used re-prompting (asking the model to fix its YAML responses), which increased the number of API calls significantly.

They then analyzed the common formatting errors, added those hints to the original prompt, and wrote an error fixing script. This reduced their errors to 0.01%.

2.  Sacrificing throughput for latency

The SDLC is dead. Long live the ADLC.

For years, software ran on the SDLC, the Software Development Lifecycle.

Plan, build, test, ship, look at the results. Even if you didn't know the name, you knew the process.

Every step existed for one reason: writing code was slow, expensive even. So everything was built around it to force alignment and reduce the cost of building wrong.

Now, that premise is gone.

Since agents write most of the diff, the build phase has collapsed to days instead of months. We need to rebuild around this new center of gravity. Agents, not code.

That's why we need the ADLC: the Agent Development Lifecycle.

Learn more: https://lnkd.in/gkebdcPy

Rest in peace, prompt engineering. If you think the key to success is the prompt, that the best engineers are the ones who learned to speak the language of the machine, I'd like to talk you out of that. The prompt matters, but not for the reason most people think. A really good prompt usually just means the person thought clearly about the problem first. Clarity is the actual skill. The prompt is only ever the symptom of having it, which means one model update and your prompting edge is gone. And the model itself is becoming a commodity too: what's being commoditized is anything that most humans can do reliably at scale. For now that feels dazzling. But dazzling is not the same as scarce.

“It’s all one big beautiful circle jerk.”

Thank you, AI researchers, for that great vision of the future.

Look, I get it. I get that they want us all in a cancer-free utopia where we live to be 200. I get that you rebranded “universal basic income” as “universal high income” to make it sound better.

But I don’t see it.

I need action.

Labs, get specific. Show me that world. Tell me how you’re measuring human flourishing that isn’t GDP. Tell me what structure or regulations you’re pushing for to set up incentives, like an automation tax or human labor benefits. Tell me anything.

outliers.text:
AI is going to uncover thousands of hidden moments in history.

Case in point: it just read a 2,000-year-old scroll burned into solid charcoal.

The Herculaneum scrolls were buried under this Roman villa when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD.

Every attempt to physically unroll them since has instantly destroyed the layers.

In 2023, a global contest called the Vesuvius Challenge launched to use AI to read the scrolls.

Researchers used high-res X-ray scans, then machine learning detected faint traces of ancient ink hidden in the fibres.

It worked. One scroll turned out to be a work on stoic philosophy.

Now the race is on to uncover hundreds more.

Moats! Does anyone have one anymore?

Yes. Yes, they do.

But only a small subset of what people call moats create real long-term value and defensibility.

In many conversations, I noticed several common misperceptions about generative AI.

- Vector search has been around since early 2010s.
- Language modeling was first introduced in 1951.

Most PMs are learning AI in the wrong order.

They try to master tools.

Claude Code. n8n. Codex. Lovable.

Sure, you need tools to build intuition and generalize. But tools change every month.

Here's the roadmap that lasts:

1. Foundations
Understand what models can and can't do.

2. Knowledge systems
Design how agents know things.

3. Agents on your own work
Use them to research, prototype, and ship.

4. Agents inside your product
Build agents that run for users and teams.

5. Trust and shipping
Make them reliable when they run without you.

6. Strategy and leadership
Turn AI capability into product advantage.

Prompt engineering is dead. Good. 

For years, the narrative was: the better your prompt, the better your AI. So everyone optimized prompts. Tried new techniques. Wrote longer context windows. Spent cycles on phrasing.

outliers.text:
How to Create a PM Second Brain in a weekend

You ship. The agent learns and builds.

Competitor pages auto-update. New hypotheses get tested. Retention insights compound across cohorts.

Step 1: set it up. 
→ Install the free pm-brain skill in Claude Code 
→ Run /pm-brain in an empty folder 
→ Answer a short interview: company, role, and current priorities 
→ It builds the folders: knowledge, hypotheses, decisions, and stakeholders 

Step 2: feed it. 
→ /ingest this weeks notes, interviews, and tickets 
→ Every claim gets tagged: documented, verbal, or your hunch 
→ Then /review sweeps it every Friday and flags what's drifting

I've been using this for eight months across Claude Code, Cowor
outliers.hook: How to Create a PM Second Brain in a weekend / You ship. The agent learns and builds.

My biggest takeaways from Rob Snyder, the author of The Power of Pull:

1. Solving a pain point isn’t enough to get people to buy your product.
2. Rob’s "PULL" framework identifies four conditions that drive a buying decision.
3. Design partners are a trap.
4. The right cold outreach message needs to be interesting, not persuasive.
5. Pull belongs to a specific person, not to a company.
6. The signal of real pull in a meeting isn’t just enthusiasm—it’s someone asking how to move forward.
7. Run the first sales call like a detective, not a pitcher.
8. When a call goes lukewarm, throw the Hail Mary.
9. Rob calls "The Case Study Factory" his most important idea.

How much will it cost to feed an accidentally overzealous AI agent’s bottomless appetite?

The cost of a single API call is plummeting. Huzzah for the future! 

And yet, your total AI bill probably went up. Why?

One reason is agentic AI. Agents make more calls overall, and those calls add up, especially with new multipliers like always-on agents and the context tax. 

Those extra calls are great when they do work that’s really useful to you. 

They’re not so great when your agent spins its wheels, goes round and round in circles, and goes nowhere. 🔄

And agentic AI is only the first reason to expect higher costs. The second separates the AI winners from everyone else.

Want to make AI adoption harder? Tell employees AI is why their colleagues are gone.

There’s a peculiar contradiction in asking people to enthusiastically embrace a technology while suggesting that successful adoption may make them disposable.

Yet “because AI” has become an awfully fashionable explanation for layoffs. The trouble is that a workforce isn’t merely a collection of tasks waiting to be automated.

It contains institutional knowledge, relationships, judgment, coordination, and trust. 

Remove those carelessly and you may discover that the shiny new complex system requires rather a lot of them.

Which helps explain why 55% of employers reportedly regret AI-driven layoffs.

↳ Have a cheap worker read it instead and hand back only the answer.

posts.text:
Claude Beginner vs Claude Professional.
The same 10 choices. How I run it as a PM:

1. Effort
→ Beginner: medium or high, never extra or max
→ Professional: extra by default (xhigh in Claude Code). In my test, it thought about as much as medium on simple questions (median 21 vs 23.5 thinking tokens) and more only on open-ended hard questions, when I needed it the most.

2. Models
→ Beginner: one model for everything
→ Professional: tell Claude it can delegate to subagents on cheaper models. It protects its context and cuts the cost.

3. Setup
→ Beginner: skip the setup, just prompt
→ Professional: the setup is the job. Context, instructions and tools decide what Claude can do for you.

posts.text:
Your AI agent is a new hire.
Most PMs skip the onboarding.

Anthropic's own advice: "Think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows."

So imagine a person joining your team on Monday:

→ The person you hire = the model
→ The onboarding doc = instructions
→ The team playbooks = skills
→ System access = connectors
→ Their notes = memory
→ Who they delegate to = subagents
→ Sign-off rules = permissions
→ The performance review = evals

Most of this is plain text. You can write it without touching code. The rest is your clicks.

Start with the onboarding doc: who we are, how we work, why it matters, and where to find more. It goes to AGENTS.md.

Spoke at The AI Conference this week and did not give a talk about what AI can do. Nobody needs another one of those.

✨Where does AI get to decide, and where does it absolutely not?
✨What happens when it's wrong? (It will be wrong.)
✨How do you know it's good, beyond "the demo looked great"?

You have to be great at AI AND great at pro

My top 5 takeaways from Nate at Anthropic on how to get Claude to design without AI slop:

1. Give Claude context upfront.

Share screenshots, pages you like, and your past work. For an existing product, have Claude rebuild the real screens from code.

2. Research familiar UX patterns.

For hard layout problems, ask Claude to research familiar products that solve something similar and note the layouts people already know how to use.

3. Make Claude aware of its design biases.

"The model has no idea what its own biases are." In your design.md or another file, consider discouraging Claude's tells like serif text, off-white backgrounds, and card-edge bars.

4. Start with wireframes.

posts.text:
I think there is too much concern expressed about the need for human verification of AI output in everyday work due to a risk of factual errors. It used to be true, but data on more recent models suggest they beat human experts in finding facts & checking claims. AIs may still underperform humans in error rates in some cases, of course, but we need to update our assumptions about how often that occurs.

And there are things to verify beyond errors - points of view, opinions, approaches, etc. But the idea that the job of humans should be checking AI work for mistakes is likely already not true today, and good riddance.

I see a lot of attempts to measure AI productivity gains in the economy using the release of ChatGPT in 2022 as a starting point. LinkedIn has published one of the best reports I’ve read on deploying LLM applications: what worked and what didn’t.

1. Structured outputs
They chose YAML over JSON as the output format because YAML uses less output tokens. Initially, only 90% of the outputs are correctly formatted YAML. They used re-prompting (asking the model to fix its YAML responses), which increased the number of API calls significantly.

They then analyzed the common formatting errors, added those hints to the original prompt, and wrote an error fixing script. This reduced their errors to 0.01%.

In many conversations, I noticed several common misperceptions about generative AI.

1. Technologies behind generative AI are new
While many applications made possible by GenAI are new, the technologies surrounding it are not.

- Retrieval, the backbone of RAG, is also the backbone of search and recommender systems. The first information retrieval system was described in the 1920s.
- Vector search has been around since early 2010s.
- Language modeling was first introduced in 1951.
- The attention mechanism was introduced in 2015.
- Inference optimization techniques (quantization, low-rank factorization, distillation) have been around for a while.

Very useful tips on tool use and memory from Manus's context engineering blog post. Key takeaways:

1. Reversible compact summary

Most models allow 128K context, which can easily fill up after a few turns when working with data like PDFs or web pages.

When the context gets full, they have to compact it. It’s important to compact the context so that it’s reversible. Eg, removing the content of a file/web page if the path/URL is kept.

2. Tool use

Given how easy it is to add new tools (e.g., with MCP servers), the number of tools a user adds to an agent can explode. Too many tools make it easier for the agent to choose the wrong action, making them dumber.

New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with Cerebras and taught by Zhenwei Gao, Sebastian Duerr, and Sarah Chieng.

When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units.

Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster

Today we’re introducing ParseBench-2 - our most ambitious document parsing benchmark to date.

It is the only benchmark that provides both extreme granularity into every single type of production parsing error, while also making sure that metric scores are highly aligned with human judgment. We do this by painstakingly assigning severity scores to 330+ error types, and tuning each metric to match the severity scores. 
Existing benchmarks either use brittle deterministic metrics (e.g. OmniDocBench) or LLM-as-a-judge (ParseArena), which can help recognize equivalent representations but are coarse/stochastic/subject to bias by the prompt+model.

One of the hardest parts around document parsing is parsing complex tables. 

Besides the task itself being difficult, it is also hard to measure what ‘good’ looks like. Ultimately it comes down to intuition around what is a catastrophic error for downstream knowledge work.
* Formatting differences (markdown vs. html tags) are harmless
* Making the header row a “data” row is also probably harmless (any human/model can interpret it as the header anyways) 
* Swapping the signs on a number, particular in financial reporting, is much more severe.

We launched ParseBench-2 last week as a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate all dimensions of document parsing: reading order, formatting, tables, charts, forms, and visual grounding.

While we strive to create some standardization, it's very clear that not everyone weights the same errors equally:
- If you're dealing with backoffice paperwork, you probably don't care about charts, and mostly care about tables and forms
- If you're not dealing with legal documents, you likely don't care about precise formatting.

You shouldn’t blindly trust benchmarks - you should be able to encode your preferences relative to your use cases and design eval metrics around that.

We’re excited to release ParseBench-2 as not only a comprehensive document parsing benchmark, but also a framework for parsing benchmark design. Where you can articulate a set of human preferences of what “good parsing” looks like and “hillclimb” evaluation metrics against that.

The important part is not hand-crafting a deterministic parsing metric. Metric design can be automated by coding agents; what’s important is an open framework + datasets for encoding human preferences and optimizing metrics.

posts.text:
Parsing forms is a hard problem, whether with specialized OCR or frontier models.

There is no standardization across various form templates. There are multiple form elements (e.g. checkboxes, signatures, text fields) that need to be represented in various ways. A good parser needs to both extract empty/filled form values along with exact bounding boxes.

We’ve spent time carefully crafting a forms dataset within ParseBench-2. It consists of 600 pages from 244 government form templates across 30 countries, with 20K annotated fields (text, checkboxes, signatures).

AI is going to uncover thousands of hidden moments in history.

Case in point: it just read a 2,000-year-old scroll burned into solid charcoal.

The Herculaneum scrolls were buried under this Roman villa when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD.

Every attempt to physically unroll them since has instantly destroyed the layers.

In 2023, a global contest called the Vesuvius Challenge launched to use AI to read the scrolls.

Researchers used high-res X-ray scans, then machine learning detected faint traces of ancient ink hidden in the fibres.

It worked. One scroll turned out to be a work on stoic philosophy.

Now the race is on to uncover hundreds more.

posts.text:
I have one rule before I’m allowed to automate anything with AI.

It's one of my most unpopular takes:

I have to do it manually at least 3 times first.

Every automation I’ve shared across socials has followed this rule. I ran my Friday “factory inspections” by hand for months before handing them to an agent.

When you do a task yourself a few times, you learn what good looks like, which steps actually matter, and where things tend to go wrong.

That’s also what lets you check an agent’s work later instead of blindly trusting it.

It also fixes the most common mistake I see when people start building with AI: going into the tools looking for problems to solve.

The people succeeding with AI

How much will it cost to feed an accidentally overzealous AI agent’s bottomless appetite?

The cost of a single API call is plummeting. Huzzah for the future! 

And yet, your total AI bill probably went up. Why?

One reason is agentic AI. Agents make more calls overall, and those calls add up, especially with new multipliers like always-on agents and the context tax. 

Those extra calls are great when they do work that’s really useful to you. 

They’re not so great when your agent spins its wheels, goes round and round in circles, and goes nowhere. 🔄

And agentic AI is only the first reason to expect higher costs. The second separates the AI winners from everyone else.

It contains institutional knowledge, relationships, judgment, coordination, and trust.

2) Learning about great writing (turns out, writing is a skill, and skills are learnable)

Enjoyed this recent podcast episode that two of the GrokBot team members had with Garry Tan and the YC crew. I got introduced to GrokBot by my son (who's a big fan). It's really well done.

Here's the quote I loved:

"Our goal is not to rebuild all of B2B SaaS. Other companies are doing a great job there. Our goal is to build the thing that can access those tools and work inside of them, and just fit naturally into the way a company already works."

~ Roman Ugarte

This is the future of HubSpot.  The GTM infrastructure you need, available headlessly, wherever you need it be in Claude, ChatGPT or one of the new AI personal agents.

The Economist has just released data showing that the AI jobs prediction so far is playing out the opposite of what many thought.

The reason this is happening is because AI is bringing automation to areas that don’t have finite demand characteristics. AI allows companies to do far more than they could before, but agents still require human operators and oversight to generate value from them. 

And not only has AI not replaced many of the types of jobs that theoretically would have been most affected by AI - engineers or lawyers - but AI is also creating or growing entire categories of jobs across the economy.
